meta.name: LENS Structure Explorer
meta.purpose: Human-curated grammar reference. Knowledge layer only — no scoring, no readiness, no assessment.
meta.source: EAQUALS Grammar Inventory (canonical) + standard CEFR grammar reference + corpus-verified examples.
meta.coverage: Canonical EAQUALS grammar inventory (~45 structures across A1-C1).

egp_keying.purpose: Detection layer -> EGP reference. Each structure keys to one or more grammar-bank family_ids (grammar_profile.json sub_categories). Turns the formation patterns into the analyser's detection source (Block 1.2 / Block 2.6).
egp_keying.level_authority: EGP is authoritative: at detection, resolve to the specific matched EGP structure and report ITS level (e.g. 'should - B1'), not the explorer's typically_introduced/common_extension range (which stays a display hint).
egp_keying.bundle: egp_bundle=true means the entry covers >1 distinct EGP structure (e.g. modals-obligation = must/should/have to); resolve to whichever matched.
egp_keying.flagged: egp_key_status='keyed_imperfect' = no exact EGP family exists for this concept; the key is the closest available and needs review (wish, inversion, verb-to-be, intensifiers, concessive-clauses, adverbial-phrases).
egp_keying.cross_cutting: egp_cross_cutting=true = the concept spans several EGP families with no single dedicated home (wish, inversion, verb-to-be, concessive-clauses, intensifiers, adverbs). Keys verified against where matching structures actually live in the bank (distinctive-marker check, 2026-08-04).

twin_resolutions.method: Where a keyed family had a near-twin (shared sub_category or near-identical name), both were checked by distinctive-marker match against grammar_profile; the family whose structures actually contain the concept was kept. Verified 2026-08-04.
twin_resolutions.adverbs_TRAP: The bank family `adverbs` holds RESPONSE TOKENS (yeah/right), NOT manner/comment adverbs — an id whose contents contradict its name. Manner/comment + frequency + position adverbs live in adverbs_and_adverb_phrases_types_and_meanings / adverbs_as_modifiers / adverbs__position, which is what adverbs, adverbs-of-frequency and adverbial-phrases are keyed to.
kept_both_twins: prepositional+prepostions (note: prepostions is a misspelled family_id)
twin_resolutions.aspectual_twins: present/past perfect, present/past perfect continuous, present_simple vs present_simple_for_future_use — disambiguated by name (present vs past; simple vs future-use); each explorer keyed to its own family.

egp_keying.single_source: structures.json is the single source of family keys; src/lib/egpFamilies.ts resolves them and asserts at module load that grammarDetect fires nothing undeclared.

keyable_pass.rule: A family is KEYABLE when an existing heading already names that language; ORPHANED when no heading names it at all. Orphaned families are shown on the Explorer under "Additional EGP families", never merged into the 45.

structures.name: Present Simple

overview.short_description: Used for facts, habits, routines, and permanent situations.

formation.notes: Third person singular adds -s/-es.

communicative_functions.example: I usually walk to work.

communicative_functions.description: State a view as a fact.
communicative_functions.example: I think it is fair.

related_gse_objectives: Can describe daily routines
Can state facts about themselves

related_structures.notes: Present simple for habits; present continuous for actions happening now.
Frequency adverbs commonly taught with the present simple.

structures.name: Present Continuous

overview.short_description: Used for actions happening now or around now, and some future arrangements.

formation.notes: Also used for future arrangements (present continuous for future).

communicative_functions.example: The children are playing outside.

related_gse_objectives: Can describe what is happening now

related_structures.notes: Habits vs. actions in progress.
Present continuous can express planned future arrangements.

structures.name: Past Simple

overview.short_description: Used to describe completed actions and events in the past.
examples: I went to the cinema yesterday.
They finished the project last week.

formation.notes: Regular verbs add -ed; irregular verbs have unique forms (go→went).

communicative_functions.example: I went to the party yesterday.

related_gse_objectives: Can describe past events
Can narrate completed actions

related_structures.notes: Past simple for finished events; present perfect for recent or relevant events.
Past simple for completed actions; past continuous for actions in progress.
Past simple for the main narrative; past perfect for earlier events.

structures.name: Past Continuous

overview.short_description: Used for actions in progress at a moment in the past, often interrupted by another event.
examples: I was reading when she called.
They were waiting at the station.

formation.notes: Often paired with the past simple for interruptions (when/while).

communicative_functions.description: Set the scene or describe an ongoing past action.
communicative_functions.example: While I was studying, the phone rang.

related_gse_objectives: Can describe simultaneous past actions

related_structures.notes: Interrupted action (continuous) vs. the interrupting event (simple).

structures.name: Present Perfect

overview.short_description: Used for past actions with present relevance, experiences, and unfinished time.
examples: She has just finished her homework.

formation.notes: Used with for/since, just/already/yet, ever/never.

communicative_functions.description: Talk about life experiences without a specific time.
communicative_functions.example: I have travelled a lot.

related_gse_objectives: Can describe experiences
Can talk about recent events

related_structures.notes: Finished time + specific moment (simple) vs. relevance to now (perfect).
Result/experience (perfect) vs. duration of an ongoing activity (perfect continuous).

structures.name: Present Perfect Continuous

overview.short_description: Used to emphasise the duration of an activity continuing up to now.
examples: I have been working all day.
It has been raining for hours.

formation.notes: Often with for/since to show duration.

communicative_functions.description: Stress how long an activity has lasted.
communicative_functions.example: She has been studying English for three years.

related_gse_objectives: Can emphasise the duration of recent activities

related_structures.notes: Completion/result vs. ongoing duration.

structures.name: Past Perfect

overview.short_description: Used for an action completed before another point in the past.
examples: By the time I arrived, they had left.
She had already eaten when I called.

formation.notes: Shows the earlier of two past events.

communicative_functions.example: When I arrived, the train had already gone.

common_chunks: By the time + past simple, past perfect

related_gse_objectives: Can sequence past events with clarity

related_structures.notes: Main narrative (simple) vs. earlier background event (perfect).

structures.name: Future: will & going to

metadata.eaquals_ref: Grammar Inventory: Future time (will and going to) (A2)

overview.short_description: Used for predictions, decisions, intentions, and plans.

positive.pattern: Subject + will + base verb | Subject + am/is/are going to + base verb
positive.example: It will rain | It is going to rain

negative.pattern: Subject + won't + base verb | ... not going to ...

question.pattern: Will + subject + base verb? | Am/Is/Are + subject + going to + base verb?

formation.notes: 'will' for spontaneous decisions/predictions; 'going to' for intentions/evidence.

communicative_functions.example: It will probably be cold.

related_gse_objectives: Can make predictions
Can talk about plans and intentions

related_structures.notes: Arrangements can also use present continuous.
1st conditional uses 'will' for results.

structures.name: Comparatives & Superlatives

overview.short_description: Used to compare two or more things.
examples: This book is longer than that one.
It is the best film of the year.

positive.pattern: adj+er / more + adj (comparative); the + adj+est / most + adj (superlative)
positive.example: bigger / more interesting; the biggest / the most interesting

formation.notes: Short adjectives add -er/-est; longer ones use more/most. Irregulars: good→better→best.

communicative_functions.example: The new phone is faster than the old one.

related_gse_objectives: Can compare people, places and things

related_structures.notes: Degree with very/too/enough vs. comparison with -er/more … than.
Adverbs compare the same way: more quickly, faster.

structures.name: Modals of Obligation (must / have to / should)

metadata.eaquals_ref: Grammar Inventory: Modals - have to / should / must (A1–B1)

overview.short_description: Used to express obligation, necessity, prohibition, and advice.

negative.pattern: mustn't (prohibition) / don't have to (no obligation) / shouldn't (advice)
negative.example: You mustn't smoke / You don't have to come

question.pattern: Do you have to + base verb? / Should I + base verb?

formation.notes: 'mustn't' = prohibited; 'don't have to' = not necessary — an important contrast.

communicative_functions.example: Employees must sign in.
You should see a doctor.

related_gse_objectives: Can express obligation and necessity
Can give advice

related_structures.notes: 'must' also expresses deduction ('he must be tired').

structures.name: Modals of Deduction (must / can't / might)

metadata.eaquals_ref: Grammar Inventory: Modals - must/can't deduction; might/may (B1/B2)

overview.short_description: Used to express how certain we are about something.

formation.notes: Past deduction: must have / can't have / might have + past participle.

communicative_functions.example: The lights are off — they must have left.
She might be late.

related_gse_objectives: Can speculate and make deductions

related_structures.notes: Same modal forms; different meaning (obligation vs. deduction).

structures.name: Conditionals: Zero & First

overview.short_description: Used for general truths (zero) and likely future results (first).
examples: If you heat water, it boils.
If you study, you will pass.

positive.pattern: If + present simple, present simple (zero) | If + present simple, will + base verb (first)
positive.example: If it rains, we stay in | If it rains, we will stay in

negative.example: If you don't hurry, we'll be late

question.pattern: What will you do if + present?
question.example: What will you do if it rains?

formation.notes: Comma when the if-clause comes first.

communicative_functions.example: If you press this, the machine starts.

related_gse_objectives: Can talk about real conditions and consequences

related_structures.notes: Real (likely) vs. hypothetical/unreal conditions.

structures.name: Conditionals: Second & Third

overview.short_description: Used for hypothetical present/future (second) and unreal past (third).
examples: If I had more time, I would travel.
If I had known, I would have helped.

positive.pattern: If + past simple, would + base verb (2nd) | If + past perfect, would have + past participle (3rd)
positive.example: If I won, I would buy a house | If I had won, I would have bought a house

negative.example: If I knew, I wouldn't ask

question.pattern: What would you do if + past simple?
question.example: What would you do if you won?

formation.notes: Second = imaginary now/future; third = regrets about the past.

communicative_functions.example: If I were you, I would apologise.

common_chunks: If I were you, I would…
If + past perfect, would have + past participle

related_gse_objectives: Can talk about hypothetical and unreal situations

related_structures.notes: Likely conditions vs. hypothetical ones.

structures.name: The Passive

overview.short_description: Used to focus on the action or its receiver rather than the doer.
examples: The report was written last week.

positive.pattern: Subject + be (correct tense) + past participle (+ by + agent)

formation.notes: The agent (by…) is often omitted when unknown or unimportant.

communicative_functions.example: The bridge was built in 1890.

related_gse_objectives: Can describe processes and procedures

related_structures.notes: Passive is built on 'be' + past participle — secure 'be' forms first.
Both reuse the past participle; 'has been taken' combines them.
Both are hallmarks of formal, impersonal register (news, reports).

structures.name: Relative Clauses

overview.short_description: Used to add information about a noun using who, which, that, whose, where.
examples: The man who lives next door is a teacher.
The book, which was long, was interesting.

formation.notes: Defining clauses identify the noun (no commas); non-defining add extra info (commas).

communicative_functions.description: Identify or add detail about a noun.
communicative_functions.example: She's the colleague who helped me.

related_gse_objectives: Can give detailed descriptions using relative clauses

related_structures.notes: Reuses wh-words (who, which, whose) in statement word order.
Both embed a clause inside another; relatives modify a noun.
The relative pronoun replaces a repeated personal pronoun.

structures.name: Reported Speech

overview.short_description: Used to report what someone said, usually with a tense shift back.
examples: He told me he had finished.

positive.pattern: Subject + reporting verb (+ that) + clause (tense shifted back)

question.example: She asked if I was ready

formation.notes: Pronouns, tenses, and time references usually shift (now→then, today→that day).

communicative_functions.example: He explained that the office was closed.

related_gse_objectives: Can report what others have said

related_structures.notes: Backshift needs secure past forms: 'I like it' → she said she liked it.
Backshift destination: past simple reports as past perfect.
Reported questions drop inversion: 'Where is it?' → asked where it was.

structures.name: Coordinating Conjunctions

metadata.eaquals_ref: Grammar Inventory: Connecting words: and, but, because (A1)

overview.short_description: Join words, phrases, or clauses of equal weight (and, but, or, so).

positive.example: I was tired, so I went home

formation.notes: Joins equal elements; for contrast/cause subordinators see related structures.

communicative_functions.example: The book was long, but interesting.
It rained, so we stayed in.

related_gse_objectives: Can link ideas with simple connectors

related_structures.notes: 'but' (A2) develops into 'although' (B1) for contrast.

structures.name: Concessive Clauses (although / though)

metadata.eaquals_ref: Grammar Inventory: Connecting words expressing contrast (B1)

overview.short_description: Subordinate clauses that express contrast or concession.
examples: Although it was cold, we went out.
She passed, even though she hadn't studied.

positive.example: Although it rained, we enjoyed it

negative.example: Although he didn't try, he won

formation.notes: More formal than 'but'; the clause can come first or second.

communicative_functions.example: Although the film was long, I enjoyed it.

related_gse_objectives: Can express contrast using subordination

related_structures.notes: Develops from 'but' (A2).
A type of subordinate clause.

structures.name: Subordination (because / when / if …)

metadata.eaquals_ref: Grammar Inventory: Connecting words expressing cause and effect, contrast etc. (B1)

overview.short_description: Linking a dependent clause to a main clause to show reason, time, condition, or contrast.
examples: We stayed home because it was raining.
When the bell rang, the class ended.

positive.pattern: Subordinator + clause + main clause (or main clause + subordinator + clause)
positive.example: Because it was late, we left

negative.example: When I didn't reply, she called

formation.notes: Common subordinators: because, since, as (reason); when, while, after, before (time); if, unless (condition); although (contrast).

communicative_functions.example: I left early because I was tired.
When I arrived, they were eating.

related_gse_objectives: Can link ideas using subordination

related_structures.notes: Concessive clauses are a kind of subordination.

structures.name: Gerunds & Infinitives

overview.short_description: Using -ing forms and to-infinitives after certain verbs and prepositions.

negative.pattern: verb + not + -ing / not to + base verb

formation.notes: Some verbs take -ing (enjoy, avoid), some take to (want, decide), some both with a meaning change (stop, remember).

communicative_functions.example: I prefer working from home.

related_gse_objectives: Can talk about preferences and plans

related_structures.notes: 'would like' + to-infinitive vs. 'like' + -ing.
'used to go' (infinitive) vs. 'be used to going' (-ing) — classic confusion pair.
After a preposition the verb takes -ing: interested in learning.

structures.name: Questions (Wh- & Yes/No)

overview.short_description: Forming yes/no and wh- questions with auxiliaries and question words.

question.pattern: Auxiliary + subject + base verb? | Wh- + auxiliary + subject + verb?
question.example: Are you ready? / Where are you?

formation.notes: Use do/does/did as auxiliaries in the present and past simple.

communicative_functions.example: What does this word mean?

related_gse_objectives: Can ask and answer simple questions

related_structures.notes: Questions with 'be' invert directly (Are you…?) — the entry point before do-support.
Tags reuse the same auxiliary system in miniature.
Reported questions lose the inversion.

structures.name: Imperatives

overview.short_description: Used to give instructions, orders, directions, and invitations.

formation.notes: Add 'please' for politeness; 'Let's + base verb' for suggestions.

communicative_functions.example: Turn left at the corner.

related_gse_objectives: Can give simple instructions and directions

related_structures.notes: 'You must/should…' as softer alternatives to a direct command.
'Can/Could you…?' turns a command into a polite request.

structures.name: Phrasal Verbs

metadata.eaquals_ref: Grammar Inventory: Phrasal verbs - common / extended (A2–C1)

overview.short_description: Verb + particle combinations whose meaning is often idiomatic.
examples: I get on well with my colleagues.

positive.pattern: Verb + particle (+ object); separable verbs can split
positive.example: turn it off / look after the children

formation.notes: Some are separable (turn it off), some inseparable (look after them).

communicative_functions.example: I get up at seven and set off at eight.

related_gse_objectives: Can use common phrasal verbs in everyday contexts

related_structures.notes: Particle vs. preposition: 'look up the word' vs. 'look at the word'.
Object pronouns split separable verbs: pick it up, not *pick up it.

structures.name: Adverbs of Frequency

overview.short_description: Show how often something happens (always, usually, sometimes, never).

positive.example: I usually walk / She is usually busy

formation.notes: Frequency adverbs go before the main verb but after 'be'.

communicative_functions.description: Say how often you do things.
communicative_functions.example: I sometimes work at weekends.

related_gse_objectives: Can describe how often they do things

related_structures.notes: Taught together with the present simple for routines.

structures.name: The Verb 'to be'

metadata.eaquals_ref: Grammar Inventory: To be, including questions and negatives (A1)

overview.short_description: The verb 'be' for identity, description, age, and location.

formation.notes: Contractions: I'm, you're, isn't, aren't.

communicative_functions.example: I am from Spain.
The box is empty.

related_gse_objectives: Can give basic personal information

related_structures.notes: 'be' vs. ordinary present-simple verbs.

structures.name: There is / There are

overview.short_description: Says that something exists or is present.
examples: There is a book on the table.

question.example: Is there a bank near here?

formation.notes: 'is' for singular/uncountable, 'are' for plural.

communicative_functions.example: There are many shops in the city.

related_gse_objectives: Can describe what is in a place

related_structures.notes: Often taught with some/any and much/many.

structures.name: Personal Pronouns

overview.short_description: Subject and object pronouns that replace nouns.

formation.notes: Subject: I/you/he/she/it/we/they; object: me/you/him/her/it/us/them.

communicative_functions.description: Refer to people without repeating names.
communicative_functions.example: This is my sister; she is a doctor.

related_gse_objectives: Can refer to people using pronouns

related_structures.notes: Possessive adjectives/pronouns relate to personal pronouns.

structures.name: Possessives ('s & possessive adjectives)

overview.short_description: Shows belonging with 's and my/your/his/her etc.

formation.notes: Plural nouns take s' (the students' room).

communicative_functions.example: My brother's name is Tom.

related_gse_objectives: Can express possession

related_structures.notes: Possessive adjectives pair with personal pronouns.

structures.name: Prepositions (place, time, movement)

metadata.eaquals_ref: Grammar Inventory: Prepositions of place/time, including in/on/at (A1)

overview.short_description: Show place, time, and direction (in, on, at, to, from).
examples: The keys are on the table.

question.example: Where is it? In the box.

formation.notes: Time: at (clock), on (days), in (months/years).

communicative_functions.example: The bank is next to the station.

related_gse_objectives: Can say where and when things are

related_structures.notes: Used together to describe places.

structures.name: Articles (a / an / the)

metadata.eaquals_ref: Grammar Inventory: Articles with countable and uncountable nouns (A2)

overview.short_description: Definite and indefinite reference with nouns.
examples: I saw a dog. The dog was friendly.

positive.pattern: a/an + singular countable | the + specific | zero article + general
positive.example: a book / the sun / dogs bark

formation.notes: 'a/an' = first mention; 'the' = already known/unique.

communicative_functions.description: Refer to general vs. specific things.
communicative_functions.example: I need a pen. The pen on your desk is fine.

related_gse_objectives: Can use articles appropriately

related_structures.notes: Articles and quantifiers both determine nouns.

structures.name: Quantifiers (much/many, some/any)

metadata.eaquals_ref: Grammar Inventory: How much/how many; much/many; countable & uncountable (A1/A2)

overview.short_description: Express quantity with countable and uncountable nouns.
examples: How many books do you have?

formation.notes: many/few = countable; much/little = uncountable; some (positive), any (questions/negatives).

communicative_functions.example: There are a few apples left.

related_gse_objectives: Can talk about quantities

related_structures.notes: Both determine the noun phrase.

structures.name: Demonstratives (this/that/these/those)

metadata.eaquals_ref: Grammar Inventory: Adjectives - common and demonstrative (A1)

overview.short_description: Point to things by distance and number.

formation.notes: this/these = near; that/those = far.

communicative_functions.example: Can I try this jacket on?

related_gse_objectives: Can point out specific things

related_structures.notes: Demonstratives are determiners like articles.

structures.name: Intensifiers (very, too, enough)

overview.short_description: Strengthen or qualify adjectives and adverbs.

formation.notes: 'too' = more than wanted; 'enough' = sufficient.

communicative_functions.example: The coffee is too hot to drink.

related_gse_objectives: Can qualify descriptions

related_structures.notes: Both modify degree of adjectives.

structures.name: Modals of Ability (can / could)

overview.short_description: Express present and past ability and possibility.

formation.notes: 'could' = past ability or polite requests.

communicative_functions.example: Can you open the window?

communicative_functions.description: State what you are able to do.
communicative_functions.example: I can speak three languages.

related_gse_objectives: Can express ability

related_structures.notes: Same modal form family.
'could' also expresses possibility.

structures.name: 'Would like' (I'd like)

overview.short_description: A polite way to express wants and offers.
examples: Would you like to sit down?

positive.pattern: Subject + would like + noun / to + verb

formation.notes: More polite than 'want'.

communicative_functions.example: I'd like the bill, please.

related_gse_objectives: Can make polite requests and offers

related_structures.notes: Both used for polite requests.

structures.name: Adverbial Phrases & Word Order

metadata.eaquals_ref: Grammar Inventory: Adverbial phrases of time, place and frequency, incl. word order (A2)

overview.short_description: Phrases of time, place, and frequency, and where they go.
examples: I go to the gym twice a week.
She arrived at the office early this morning.

positive.example: They played well at home yesterday

formation.notes: Typical order: manner - place - time.

communicative_functions.description: Say when, where, and how often.
communicative_functions.example: I usually study at home in the evening.

related_gse_objectives: Can position adverbials correctly

related_structures.notes: Frequency adverbs are part of adverbial phrasing.

structures.name: Adverbs (manner & comment)

metadata.eaquals_ref: Grammar Inventory: Adverbs; adjectives and adverbs (B1/B2)

overview.short_description: Describe how actions happen and comment on statements.

formation.notes: Most manner adverbs add -ly; irregulars: well, fast, hard.

communicative_functions.example: The team performed brilliantly.

related_gse_objectives: Can describe how actions are done

related_structures.notes: Adverbs also have comparative forms.

structures.name: Question Tags

overview.short_description: Short tags added to check or confirm information.

formation.notes: Tag uses the auxiliary of the statement and opposite polarity.

communicative_functions.example: We've met before, haven't we?

related_gse_objectives: Can check information with question tags

related_structures.notes: Tags reuse question auxiliaries.

structures.name: Future Continuous

overview.short_description: An action in progress at a future time.
examples: This time tomorrow I'll be flying to Rome.
Don't call at 8 - we'll be eating.

question.example: Will you be using the car?

formation.notes: Often with a specific future time.

communicative_functions.description: Talk about future activities in progress.
communicative_functions.example: I'll be studying all weekend.

related_gse_objectives: Can describe future actions in progress

related_structures.notes: Future forms family.
Future aspect contrast.

structures.name: Future Perfect

overview.short_description: An action completed before a point in the future.
examples: By 2030 they will have finished the bridge.

formation.notes: Usually with 'by + future time'.

communicative_functions.example: By June I will have graduated.

related_gse_objectives: Can describe completion relative to a future point

related_structures.notes: Future aspect contrast.
Perfect aspect across time frames.

structures.name: Past Perfect Continuous

overview.short_description: Emphasises the duration of an activity before a past point.
examples: She had been working there for years before she left.
They were tired because they had been running.

formation.notes: Often with for/since + past reference.

communicative_functions.description: Stress how long something had lasted.
communicative_functions.example: By noon, they had been driving for six hours.

related_gse_objectives: Can emphasise duration of earlier past activities

related_structures.notes: Perfect vs. perfect-continuous in the past.
Same aspect in present.

structures.name: 'used to' & 'would' (past habits)

metadata.eaquals_ref: Grammar Inventory: Would expressing habits in the past (B2)

overview.short_description: Describe repeated past habits and former states.
examples: I used to play football every weekend.
We would go to the seaside each summer.

positive.pattern: Subject + used to / would + base verb

negative.pattern: Subject + didn't use to + base verb
negative.example: I didn't use to like it

question.pattern: Did + subject + use to + base verb?
question.example: Did you use to live here?

formation.notes: 'would' for repeated actions, not past states (use 'used to' for states).

communicative_functions.example: There used to be a cinema here.

related_gse_objectives: Can describe past habits and former states

related_structures.notes: Habitual vs. single past events.

structures.name: 'wish' / 'if only'

metadata.eaquals_ref: Grammar Inventory: Wish; Wish/if only regrets (B2/C1)

overview.short_description: Express regrets and unreal desires about present and past.
examples: I wish I had more time.
If only I had studied harder.

positive.pattern: wish + past simple (present) | wish + past perfect (past)
positive.example: I wish I knew / I wish I had known

formation.notes: 'wish + would' for annoyance about others' habits.

communicative_functions.example: I wish I could be there.

related_gse_objectives: Can express regrets and wishes

related_structures.notes: Both use unreal/backshifted tenses.

structures.name: Modals in the Past (should have / might have)

metadata.eaquals_ref: Grammar Inventory: Modals - should have/might have; modals in the past (B1/C1)

overview.short_description: Comment on, criticise, or speculate about past events.
examples: She might have missed the train.

negative.pattern: Subject + modal + not have + past participle

formation.notes: should have (criticism/regret), might/could have (past possibility), must have (past deduction).

communicative_functions.example: The ground is wet - it must have rained.
You should have booked earlier.

related_gse_objectives: Can speculate and comment on past events

related_structures.notes: Deduction extended to the past.
Third conditional uses similar forms.

structures.name: Inversion (negative adverbials)

metadata.eaquals_ref: Grammar Inventory: Inversion with negative adverbials (C1)

overview.short_description: Auxiliary-before-subject order after fronted negative adverbials for emphasis.
examples: Never have I seen such a mess.
Not only did she win, but she also broke the record.

negative.example: Under no circumstances should you leave

formation.notes: Triggers: never, rarely, seldom, not only, no sooner, little, only then.

communicative_functions.example: Not until later did we understand.

related_gse_objectives: Can use inversion for emphasis

related_structures.notes: Same auxiliary–subject inversion mechanism as questions.
Inverted conditionals: 'Had I known…' = 'If I had known…'.
Fronted negative adverbials (Never/Rarely…) are what trigger the inversion.
